Theme

coal noun

also charcoal, coals, embers (glowing coals), coal mine

classical

Cato Agr. 38; 155
Cic. Off. 2.25 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 293

carbō, carbōnis m.

noun, third declension

charcoal; coal

Classically charcoal, dead or glowing: the Romans heated and cooked with wood and charcoal. Modern Latin uses the word for coal too; where it matters, add fossilis.

Other words

  • * (our own formation) carbō fossilis — coal (mined, not made from wood)

    also used · * our formation

    Our phrase, after Varro’s sāl fossilis, rock salt, and Pliny’s ebur fossile (Lewis & Short, s.v. fossilis, “dug up”). None of the reference works has a word for mineral coal.

  • fodīna carbōnāria — a coal mine

    also used · modern · Traupman 168; Traupman 293

  • lapis gagātēs — coal (Traupman)

    avoid · modern · Traupman 293

    Traupman’s word for coal; but gagātēs is jet, a hard black stone (Plin. NH 36.141, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • in vīllā, cum pluet, circumīre oportet, sīcubi perpluat, et signāre carbōne, cum dēsierit pluere, utī tēgula mūtētur

    when it rains, you should go round the house to see where the rain comes through, and mark the place with charcoal, so that the tile can be changed when the rain stopsCato Agr. 155

See also fire, hearth.

SourcesLewis & Short: carbo · Lewis & Short: fossilis · Lewis & Short: gagates
